The presence of dimples indicates that fracture is essentially by nucleation, growth and coalescence of microvoids within the matrix.

Furthermore, the presence of primary c9 and MC carbides at the grain boundaries could have restricted the grain coarsening by grain boundary pinning effect and thereby helped in maintaining finer grain size.

The drop in ductility can be due to considerable strengthening of the alloy due to the presence of fine c9 (after aging) in the matrix and MC carbides in the form of continuous film at the grain boundaries causing grain boundary embrittlement.

The severe ductility loss at 650uC can be attributed to the increased importance of grain boundary deformation/sliding at 650 uC, which leads to the formation of grain boundary cavities and concomitant brittle fracture.

Examination by SEM of the as hipped alloy has revealed the presence of c9-Ni3 (Ti, Al) with near cuboidal morphology in the matrix and c9 with acicular morphology at the grain boundaries (Fig. 4).
The SEM image (Fig. 4) of the as hipped alloy has further revealed the MC carbides due to the presence of strong carbide formers, such as W, Ti and C, with adequate quantity in the alloy.
Superalloy U720LI powder subjected to HIP at 1200 uC/120 MPa/3 h has shown a homogeneous microstructure containing equiaxed grains with an average grain diameter of ,45 mm.
The microstructure exhibits annealing twins and is found to be free from undesirable features, such as PPB networks and intraparticle porosity.

The SEM image (Fig. 8) shows that the size and morphology of c9 in aged alloy remain essentially the same as that in solution treated condition. This may be due to the fact that the finer c9 formed during aging could not be resolved by SEM.
Furthermore, the micrograph (Fig. 8) reveals the presence of carbides in the form of a continuous film at grain boundaries, and in spheroidal form in the matrix of the aged alloy.
In addition, a large number of annealing twins have been formed during aging treatment (Fig. 7).
The as hipped alloy exhibited adequate strength and ductility at RT (Table 3) as well as at 650 uC (Table 4) and is quite comparable to those reported for the wrought alloy for creep application.

The drop in ductility can be due to considerable strengthening of the alloy due to the presence of fine c9 (after aging) in the matrix and MC carbides in the form of continuous film at the grain boundaries causing grain boundary embrittlement.

However, the increase in strength of the alloy is accompanied by a drop in tensile elongation at both the test temperatures, with its effect being more significant at 650 uC with which the ductility dropped drastically.

The severe ductility loss at 650uC can be attributed to the increased importance of grain boundary deformation/sliding at 650 uC, which leads to the formation of grain boundary cavities and concomitant brittle fracture.
